AZ-104.text: A VM scale set is configured with a scale-out rule: when average CPU > 70% for 10 minutes, increase instance count by 20%. The current instance count is 5 and maximum is 10. Average CPU reaches 80% for 12 minutes. How many instances will be running after the scale-out action?

optionRationales.A: Leaving the count at 5 would mean no scale-out happened, but the rule's condition (average CPU above 70% for 10 minutes) is satisfied at 80% over 12 minutes, so the engine does add capacity.
optionRationales.B: A 20% increase on the current 5 instances equals 1 additional instance, and 5 + 1 = 6 stays under the configured maximum of 10, so autoscale provisions exactly 6 instances.
optionRationales.C: Reaching 10 would require the percentage increase to exceed the maximum cap, but a 20% bump from 5 only yields 6, so the maximum of 10 is never approached by this single action.
optionRationales.D: Arriving at 7 implies adding 2 instances, but 20% of 5 rounds to a single instance, so the engine adds 1 rather than 2.

AZ-104.explanation: The scale-out rule increases the instance count by 20%. 20% of 5 instances = 1 additional instance. 5 + 1 = 6, which is within the configured maximum of 10. The autoscale engine calculates the new instance count as 6 and scales out to 6 instances. 10 would only apply if the increase were large enough to hit the maximum cap, which it is not in this case.

AZ-104.text: You need the lowest-cost storage redundancy option that copies critical data to a secondary Azure region for disaster recovery. Applications do not need to read from the secondary region unless a failover occurs. Which option should you choose?

optionRationales.A: LRS keeps copies within one datacenter and provides no secondary-region copy.
optionRationales.B: ZRS spreads copies across availability zones in the primary region but does not copy data to a secondary region.
optionRationales.C: GRS is the lowest-cost listed option that copies data to a secondary region when applications do not require direct secondary read access.
optionRationales.D: RA-GRS uses the same geo-replication and adds a readable secondary endpoint, which costs more and is not required by this scenario.

AZ-104.explanation: GRS copies data synchronously within the primary region using LRS and asynchronously to a secondary region. It is the lowest-cost listed option that provides a secondary-region copy when direct read access to that copy is not required. RA-GRS adds a readable secondary endpoint, ZRS stays within one region, and LRS stays within one datacenter.

AZ-104.text: Operations needs an email when a production VM stays above 90% CPU for 5 minutes. The alert should be near real time and should not require writing KQL unless necessary. Which Azure Monitor design is most appropriate?

options.text: A Log Analytics query alert paired with a runbook-driven notification workflow
A Metric alert rule with an action group containing an email action
Azure Advisor recommendations reviewed manually by operations staff
Azure Service Health alerts that only report Azure platform incidents

optionRationales.A: Log query alerts run KQL against ingested logs in a Log Analytics workspace, adding ingestion latency plus query authoring, and chaining a runbook adds orchestration overhead the scenario explicitly wants to avoid for a simple email.
optionRationales.B: Percentage CPU is a native VM platform metric, so a metric alert evaluates it directly at near-real-time frequency with no KQL or log ingestion, and an attached action group with an email action delivers the notification when the 90% threshold holds for 5 minutes.
optionRationales.C: Advisor surfaces periodic optimization and right-sizing recommendations on a batch cadence; it does not evaluate a live CPU threshold or send threshold-breach notifications.
optionRationales.D: Service Health reports Azure platform incidents and planned maintenance affecting the service itself, not customer workload metrics like a single VM's CPU utilization.

AZ-104.explanation: CPU percentage is a platform metric, so a metric alert is the simplest and most responsive approach. The notification path is handled by an action group with an email action. A log query alert adds unnecessary query and ingestion dependencies, while Advisor and Service Health solve different monitoring problems.

AZ-900.text: A company wants to migrate a line-of-business application to Azure without changing how it is deployed. The IT team must keep control of the guest operating system, install a custom monitoring agent, and manage application patching themselves. Which cloud service model best fits this requirement?

optionRationales.A: PaaS has the provider manage the operating system and platform runtime, so it does not give the team guest-OS control to install an OS-level monitoring agent. The customer still maintains its application code, updates, configuration and data; application patching alone does not distinguish PaaS from IaaS.
optionRationales.B: A managed function platform handles the underlying operating system and runtime. It does not provide the guest-OS control required to install the monitoring agent or preserve this application’s existing VM deployment model.
optionRationales.C: Infrastructure as a Service provisions virtual machines where the customer retains full control of the guest operating system, can install custom software such as a monitoring agent, and remains responsible for application patching, which matches a lift-and-shift migration that keeps the existing deployment model unchanged.
optionRationales.D: Software as a Service delivers a finished, vendor-operated application such as Microsoft 365; there is no guest OS to control, no place to install custom agents, and no application patching for the customer to own, so it cannot host a migrated line-of-business app.

AZ-900.explanation: IaaS is the best fit when the customer needs control of the guest operating system, installed software, and application patching. PaaS and FaaS remove operating system management, and SaaS provides a finished application rather than a configurable hosting environment.

AZ-900.text: Before approving a new Azure deployment, a project manager wants an estimate of the expected monthly cost for selected services, regions, and sizes. Which tool should be used?

optionRationales.A: Azure Monitor collects metrics, logs, and telemetry from resources that are already running so you can observe health and performance; it has no facility for forecasting the price of a configuration that has not yet been deployed.
optionRationales.B: The Azure Pricing Calculator is the web-based estimation tool built for exactly this pre-deployment task: you add services, then set region, SKU/tier, instance size, operating system, and usage hours, and it returns an estimated monthly cost using per-unit retail prices that update as you change parameters.
optionRationales.C: Microsoft Defender for Cloud evaluates security posture, surfaces a secure score, and protects workloads against threats; it produces no cost estimate for a planned set of services and sizes.
optionRationales.D: Azure Resource Graph runs fast queries across the inventory of resources that already exist in your subscriptions; it reports on deployed assets rather than projecting the monthly price of a proposed configuration.

AZ-900.explanation: The Azure Pricing Calculator is the web-based estimation tool used before deployment to forecast expected Azure costs. Users add services, then choose parameters such as region, SKU or tier, instance size, operating system, usage hours, and eligible savings options. Microsoft Cost Management instead analyzes, monitors, and optimizes actual cloud spending after deployment.

AZ-900.text: A team wants a managed relational database for a new Azure-hosted application. They want Microsoft to handle operating system patching, database engine updates, backups, and built-in high availability. Which service best fits?

options.text: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

optionRationales.A: This is a fully managed PaaS relational database where Microsoft operates the underlying infrastructure, applies OS and SQL Server engine patches, takes automated backups, and provides built-in high availability, so the team never administers servers. It also offers vCore and DTU purchasing models plus serverless and Hyperscale tiers to match workload needs.
optionRationales.B: This is an IaaS offering where the customer remains responsible for the guest operating system, including applying OS updates and SQL Server patches, plus configuring backups and high availability themselves. That operational burden is exactly what the team wants Microsoft to handle, so it fails the managed requirement.
optionRationales.C: This is a migration tool used to move data into Azure data platforms, not a database engine that hosts and serves a running application. It performs a one-time or staged data transfer and is not designed to be the long-term home for the application's relational data.
optionRationales.D: This is a desktop and application virtualization service that delivers Windows session hosts to end users, not a database platform. It provides no relational database engine, automated backups, or database high availability, so it cannot support the application's data tier.

AZ-900.explanation: Azure SQL Database is the fully managed PaaS option that fits this scenario. Microsoft handles the underlying infrastructure, OS patching, SQL Server engine upgrades, automated backups, and built-in high availability, so the team does not operate servers. It runs on the latest stable SQL Server engine, supports vCore and DTU purchasing, and offers serverless and Hyperscale tiers. SQL Server on Azure VMs is IaaS and would require the customer to manage the OS and SQL patches, while Database Migration Service is a tool, not a long-term database host.
